question.context: A command and control behavior was blocked on host `vnevado-win10r`, which indicated an active infection by malware that could replicate and receive commands from remote attackers. This malware was active, and precautionary measures should be taken to check for residual signs of infection. The process involved had the ID 1332 and ran the command `curl http://vectorsandarrows.com`.
question.question: What is the IP address associated with the Manatee Tempest activity group detected in this security incident?
solution: The account with SID `S-1-5-21-1840191660-8534830288-125585561-1522` was involved in a Command and Control behavior that was blocked.
The cybercriminal group known as Manatee Tempest, which is associated with the IP address `198.43.121.209`, was active during the incident.

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures question.context: A Mimikatz credential theft tool was detected on a device at 2024-07-04 22:35:03.797541+00:00. Mimikatz is a tool used to harvest plaintext passwords, password hashes, smartcard PINs, and Kerberos tickets. The attacker might be leveraging this tool to harvest credentials to log into this or other devices on the network by impersonating a valid user. Several command line executions involving `mimikatz.exe` were observed, along with connected mimikatz-related files like `mimidrv.sys`, `mimispool.dll`, and `mimilove.exe`. More information can be found in the Mimikatz tool profile Threat Analytics report and the Actor profile: Storm-0875 Threat Analytics report provided by Microsoft.

Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', question.context: A possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was detected on the host `vnevado-win10s` involving user with username `dp5hn`. The PRT is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication used to enable single sign-on (SSO) across applications on supported devices, and attackers attempting to access this resource could be aiming for lateral movement or credential theft. The attempt was carried out by the process `browsercore.exe` as observed from the process ID `2676`.

observed on this device. Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures "Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) has been detected. A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', "Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) has been detected. A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

SELECT DISTINCT ae.FileName
FROM AlertEvidence ae
JOIN SecurityAlert sa
  ON ae.AlertId = sa.SystemAlertId
WHERE sa.AlertName = 'Potentially compromised assets exhibiting ransomware-like behavior'
  AND ae.FileName IS NOT NULL
  AND ae.FileName <> ''
LIMIT 20

SELECT DISTINCT ae.FileName, ae.FolderPath, ae.DeviceName, ae.AccountUpn
FROM AlertEvidence ae
JOIN SecurityAlert sa
  ON ae.AlertId = sa.SystemAlertId
WHERE sa.AlertName = 'Possible compromised user account delivering ransomware-related files'
  AND ae.FileName IS NOT NULL
  AND ae.FileName <> ''
LIMIT 20
SELECT AlertId, Title, EntityType, FileName, DeviceName, AccountUpn, TimeGenerated FROM AlertEvidence ORDER BY TimeGenerated DESC LIMIT 20

[('Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT)', "Possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) has been detected. A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

question.context: There was a detection of unknown malware being active in the environment, which was stopped by Windows Defender but it is recommended to further check the machine for signs of infection. Following that, there were multiple alerts indicating possible attempts to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) which is a key artifact used for Azure AD authentication. Additionally, we observed an alert where system recovery settings were tampered with, indicating that adversaries might be attempting to delete or disable built-in operating system data and recovery services. This could prevent recovery of a corrupted system and denie access to backups and recovery options. Various built-in Windows utilities can be exploited to disable or delete system recovery features, posing a risk to system integrity.
question.question: What is the name of the account involved in the system recovery setting tampering incident?
solution: An unknown malware was detected and was active on the host with AadDeviceId `4d8d23e9-a77d-4e33-9435-b8c457e57ca1`.
There was a possible attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT) involving the process `browsercore.exe`.
The user with SID `S-1-5-21-1840191660-8534830288-125585561-1522` was involved in a potential attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT).
System recovery setting tampering was observed on the account named `dp5hn`.

question.context: A security incident involving the Manatee Tempest activity group was flagged, where the actor Manatee Tempest, known for its early malware campaigns like the Dridex banking trojan, has been active since June 2014. The group utilizes tactics such as drive-by downloads and FakeUpdates infections, facilitated by Mustard Tempest to gain initial access. Later, they use the BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. One of the events related to this incident involved a process running on the host `vnevado-win11t` using the command `curl http://vectorsandarrows.com`. The Process ID was 88.
question.question: There was another instance of a similar process being run on the same host in this incident. Can you identify the Process ID and the command line of this process?
solution: A user with AadUserId `731adb71-b11c-4bbf-850b-57989b350e96` was associated with suspicious activity linked to the Manatee Tempest cybercriminal group.

solution: There was a possible attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT) using the process `browsercore.exe`.
The user with AadUserId `1d94aaf6-efe6-4e76-ad56-ffd7d1257bc1` was involved in a possible attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT).

question.question: What was the URL blocked due to Command and Control (C2) behavior in this incident?

Validate the alert and scope the suspected breach.
1. Find related machines, network addresses, and files in the incident graph.
2. Check for other suspicious activities in the machine timeline.
3. Locate unfamiliar processes in the process tree. Check files for prevalence, their locations, and digital signatures.
4. Submit relevant files for deep analysis and review file behaviors. 
5. Identify unusual system activity with system owners. 

B. If you have validated the alert, contain and mitigate the breach.
1. Record relevant artifacts, including those you need in mitigation rules.
2. Stop suspicious processes. Block prevalent malware files across the network.
3. Isolate affected machines.
4. Identify potentially compromised accounts. If necessary, reset passwords and decommission accounts.
5. Block relevant emails, websites, and IP addresses. Remove attack emails from mailboxes.
6. Update antimalware signatures and run full scans.

question.context: A possible attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was detected on the host `vnevado-win11u` with AadDeviceId `bc00e484-d0e5-4da4-9472-95568cccc07e`. The process involved in this attempt was `browsercore.exe` (ProcessId: 1640), launched at `2024-06-20T09:32:12.1031042Z`. PRT is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication used for single sign-on across applications, and attackers may target it to move laterally or perform credential theft. For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report on the Microsoft Security website.
question.question: Can you provide the command line of the process that was created using WMI on the host?
solution: There was a possible attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT) associated with the Azure AD user with AadUserId `731adb71-b11c-4bbf-850b-57989b350e96`.

question.context: A security incident involving system recovery setting tampering was observed on the device with name `vnevado-win10r`. The incident involved processes `vssblatemp.exe` and `bcdedit.exe` being executed on the host `vnevado-win10r` to potentially disrupt recovery options. Additionally, suspicious hands-on keyboard user behavior was detected around the same time, which might indicate that the user has been compromised.
question.question: Following these activities, there was an indication of ransomware behavior detected in the file system on a device. Can you determine the AadDeviceId of the host where this ransomware activity was detected?
solution: The account `dp5hn` was responsible for tampering with system recovery settings.
The same host device with AadDeviceId `e5799261-6720-4297-961e-bd9ca4275033` exhibited suspicious hands-on keyboard behavior, indicating a potential user compromise.
Ransomware behavior was detected on the host with AadDeviceId `e5799261-6720-4297-961e-bd9ca4275033`, indicating potential mass encryption of files by ransomware.

('2024-06-20 09:19:23.690415+00:00', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', ('2024-06-20 09:40:00.129604+00:00', "Suspicious 'GenRansom' behavior was detected", 'Malware and unwanted software are undesirable applications that perform annoying, disruptive, or harmful actions on affected machines. Some of these undesirable applications can replicate and spread from one machine to another. ('2024-06-20 09:40:00.275880+00:00', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', question.context: An alert reported that the LSASS process memory was modified, potentially to bypass security measures. During this incident, a suspicious process `notepad.exe` was observed running on host `vnevado-win10v` with specific command line arguments. Another alert was subsequently triggered indicating that a Windows Sysinternals tool was renamed and executed.
question.question: From the subsequent alert, what was the name of the Windows Sysinternals tool that was renamed before it was launched?
solution: The LSASS process memory was modified from IP address `107.224.99.179`.
A Windows Sysinternals tool was renamed to `mimikatz.exe` and then launched, which might indicate malicious activity.

question.context: A security incident involving multiple malicious activities was detected. It started with a known credential theft tool, `mimikatz.exe`, being executed at two different times, indicating an attempt to dump users' credentials. This activity led to lateral movement attempts to the jump server and suspicious remote activities on the machine. Subsequent analysis revealed command and control behavior of malware which was blocked.
question.question: What was the URL associated with the command and control behavior detected in the end alert?
solution: A known credential theft tool execution was detected on the host with AadDeviceId `4d8d23e9-a77d-4e33-9435-b8c457e57ca1`.
There was lateral movement to the jump server from the IP address `99.83.111.100` using PSExec.
Suspicious remote activity was observed on the account `dp5hn`.
Command and Control behavior was blocked for the URL `http://vectorsandarrows.com/`.

This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]

•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]

It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

Adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating system data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]
•	Windows Management Instrumentation can be used to delete volume shadow copies using the following command: [wmic shadowcopy delete]
•	wbblatemp.exe can be used to delete the Windows Backup Catalog using the following command: [wbblatemp.exe delete catalog -quiet]
•	bcdedit.exe can be used to disable automatic Windows recovery features by modifying boot configuration data using the following command: [bcdedit.exe /set default bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures question.context: A security incident involving an attempt to access a Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was detected. The PRT is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on various devices, including Windows 10. The incident involved a device with HostName `vnevado-win10s` and AadDeviceId `f5b847aa-8712-4bf6-b4f7-ed6cd89e1505`, where the process `browsercore.exe` (ProcessId `2676` created at `2024-06-20T09:10:59.867384Z`) was running. Attackers may use this to move laterally within the organization.
question.question: Following this incident, 'CommandAndControl' malware was detected on another device during lateral movement. What is the AadDeviceId of this affected device?
solution: A possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) has been detected for the user with AadUserId `731adb71-b11c-4bbf-850b-57989b350e96`.
'CommandAndControl' malware was detected on the device with AadDeviceId `bc00e484-d0e5-4da4-9472-95568cccc07e`, indicating an attempt of lateral movement.

question.context: A security incident regarding System recovery setting tampering and possible attempts to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was reported. Specifically, there was an attempt to disable system recovery features using `vssblatemp.exe` and `bcdedit` on the host `vnevado-win11u` with a user account having the SID `S-1-5-21-1840191660-8534830288-125585561-1522`. Notably, it included a potential access of PRTs, as mentioned in the Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report.
question.question: In relation to the malicious credential theft tool execution detected in this multi-stage incident, can you identify the file name of the tool that was executed?
solution: The system recovery settings tampering was attempted by the user with AadUserId `731adb71-b11c-4bbf-850b-57989b350e96`.
An attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was detected, associated with the process `browsercore.exe`.
Another attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was detected, originating from the IP address `107.224.99.179`.
A malicious credential theft tool `mimikatz.exe` was executed.

question.context: A security incident involving the Manatee Tempest activity group was reported. This Russia-based cybercriminal group, which has been active since June 2014, is known for malware campaigns including the Dridex banking trojan. They often gain initial access through methods such as drive-by downloads and malvertising, facilitated by their partnership with Mustard Tempest. As part of this security incident, a suspicious WMI process creation was observed on the machine `vnevado-win10r`, which might be an indicator of malware using WMI to spawn new processes and further infect the machine.
question.question: Can you provide the command line details of the suspicious WMI process observed on the machine?
solution: The Russia-based cybercriminal group Manatee Tempest is involved in an activity targeting an account with SID `S-1-5-21-1840191660-8534830288-125585561-1522`.

A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. It is a JSON Web Token (JWT) that's specially issued to Microsoft first party token brokers to enable single sign-on (SSO) across the applications used on those devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

For more information, read the Activity profile: Midnight Blizzard credential attacks Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/e4aad043-a273-4f88-b65e-fdfc3996ec92/analystreport?

SELECT DISTINCT DeviceName,
                               DeviceId,
                               ProcessCommandLine,
                               InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
                               ActionType,
                               TimeGenerated
FROM DeviceProcessEvents
WHERE TimeGenerated >= '2024-07-04'
  AND TimeGenerated < '2024-07-05'
  AND (
        ProcessCommandLine LIKE '%vssblatemp.exe%'
        OR ProcessCommandLine LIKE '%bcdedit /set bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures%'
        OR ProcessCommandLine LIKE '%get-userprttoken.ps1%'
        OR InitiatingProcessCommandLine LIKE '%get-userprttoken.ps1%'
      )
ORDER BY TimeGenerated
LIMIT 200

SELECT DISTINCT DeviceName,
                               DeviceId,
                               ActionType,
                               FileName,
                               FolderPath,
                               ProcessCommandLine,
                               InitiatingProcessFileName,
                               InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
                               RemoteIP,
                               FileOriginIP,
                               TimeGenerated
FROM DeviceEvents
WHERE TimeGenerated >= '2024-07-04'
  AND TimeGenerated < '2024-07-05'
  AND (
        ProcessCommandLine LIKE '%vssblatemp.exe%'
        OR ProcessCommandLine LIKE '%delete shadows /all%'
        OR ProcessCommandLine LIKE '%bcdedit /set bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures%'
        OR ProcessCommandLine LIKE '%get-userprttoken.ps1%'
        OR InitiatingProcessCommandLine LIKE '%get-userprttoken.ps1%'
      )
ORDER BY TimeGenerated
LIMIT 200

SELECT 'DeviceProcessEvents' AS SrcTable,
       TimeGenerated,
       DeviceName,
       ProcessCommandLine,
       InitiatingProcessCommandLine
FROM DeviceProcessEvents
WHERE ProcessCommandLine LIKE '%vssblatemp.exe%'
   OR InitiatingProcessCommandLine LIKE '%vssblatemp.exe%'
UNION ALL
SELECT 'DeviceEvents' AS SrcTable,
       TimeGenerated,
       DeviceName,
       ProcessCommandLine,
       InitiatingProcessCommandLine
FROM DeviceEvents
WHERE ProcessCommandLine LIKE '%vssblatemp.exe%'
   OR InitiatingProcessCommandLine LIKE '%vssblatemp.exe%'
UNION ALL
SELECT 'DeviceFileEvents' AS SrcTable,
       TimeGenerated,
       DeviceName,
       InitiatingProcessCommandLine AS ProcessCommandLine,
       NULL AS InitiatingProcessCommandLine
FROM DeviceFileEvents
WHERE InitiatingProcessCommandLine LIKE '%vssblatemp.exe%'
UNION ALL
SELECT 'AlertEvidence' AS SrcTable,
       TimeGenerated,
       DeviceName,
       ProcessCommandLine,
       NULL AS InitiatingProcessCommandLine
FROM AlertEvidence
WHERE ProcessCommandLine LIKE '%vssblatemp.exe%'
ORDER BY TimeGenerated
LIMIT 200

SELECT TimeGenerated,
       AlertId,
       Title,
       ThreatFamily,
       DeviceName,
       ProcessCommandLine,
       RemoteIP,
       RemoteUrl,
       FileName,
       FolderPath
FROM AlertEvidence
WHERE (ThreatFamily LIKE '%ransom%' OR Title LIKE '%ransom%' OR AttackTechniques LIKE '%ransom%')
   OR (ProcessCommandLine LIKE '%vssblatemp.exe%' OR ProcessCommandLine LIKE '%get-userprttoken.ps1%' OR ProcessCommandLine LIKE '%bcdedit /set bootstatuspolicy ignoreallfailures%')
ORDER BY TimeGenerated
LIMIT 200

question.context: A security incident involving suspected tampering with system recovery settings using various commands and processes, including `vssblatemp.exe` to delete all volume shadow copies, was observed on device `vnevado-win11t` (AAD Device ID: `e5799261-6720-4297-961e-bd9ca4275033`). During the incident, the process `vssblatemp.exe` was executed with command: `vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all`. This is part of an adversarial attempt to prevent the recovery of corrupted systems by deleting built-in operating system data or turning off recovery services. The incident was detected on 2024-07-04. This tampering could deny access to available backups and recovery options, augmenting the effects of data destruction or data encryption.
question.question: Can you identify the executable file name of the process that attempted to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT) as part of the related alerts?
solution: There was system recovery setting tampering by the Azure AD user with AadUserId `731adb71-b11c-4bbf-850b-57989b350e96`.
There was a possible attempt to access the Primary Refresh Token (PRT) involving the process `browsercore.exe`.

question.context: A Mimikatz credential theft tool was detected on a device. Mimikatz is a credential theft tool that can harvest plaintext passwords, password hashes, smartcard PINs, and Kerberos tickets. Attackers may use this tool to harvest credentials to log into this or other devices on the network by impersonating a valid user. The detection of Mimikatz is part of a broader security investigation. Additionally, there was later evidence of lateral movement to the jump server `Vnevado-jump` using PSExec.
question.question: A related alert indicated a possible compromised user account dropping ransomware-related files. Can you identify the name of the specific file associated with the ransomware activity?
solution: The Mimikatz credential theft tool was detected on the device with AadDeviceId `4d8d23e9-a77d-4e33-9435-b8c457e57ca1`.
Lateral movement to the jump server occurred using PSExec to IP address `99.83.111.100`.
A compromised user account was observed dropping a ransomware-related file named `get-userprttoken.ps1` on several devices.

('2024-06-20 09:19:23.690415+00:00', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

('2024-06-20 09:40:00.756601+00:00', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.

Operating systems may contain features that can help fix corrupted systems, such as a backup catalog, volume shadow copies, and automatic repair features. Adversaries may stop or delete system recovery features to augment the effects of Data Destruction and Data Encrypted for Impact.

Many native Windows utilities have been used by adversaries to disable or delete system recovery features:
•	 vssblatemp.exe can be used to delete all volume shadow copies on a system using the following command: [vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all /quiet]

Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

question.context: A security incident involving the Manatee Tempest activity group was detected. This group is known for using drive-by downloads and other methods to gain initial access, followed by using malware tools for lateral movement. The incident started with a suspicious activity involving a URL `http://vectorsandarrows.com`, accessed from host `vnevado-win10r` with IP address `198.43.121.209` via a curl command. The ProcessId__CreatedTimeUtc__CommandLine is `1332__2024-06-20t09:10:52.7298237z__curl http://vectorsandarrows.com`.
question.question: What is the host name of the device where 'CommandAndControl' malware was detected during lateral movement?
solution: Manatee Tempest, a Russia-based cybercriminal group, was involved in the use of access broker Mustard Tempest to facilitate infections and lateral movement using BLISTER loader and Cobalt Strike beacons on various networks. The group used domain fronting for command-and-control of Cobalt Strike.
A suspicious account with SID `S-1-5-21-1840191660-8534830288-125585561-1522` was identified in the context of the Manatee Tempest group activities.
The 'CommandAndControl' malware was detected on the host `vnevado-win10s`, indicating an attempt at lateral movement within the network.

The group also employs domain fronting for command-and-control channels.

question.context: A security incident related to the Manatee Tempest activity group has been detected. This actor, tracked by Microsoft and known to be a Russia-based cybercriminal group, has been active since June 2014 and is notorious for its Dridex banking trojan campaigns. The group partners with Mustard Tempest to facilitate access to target networks via methods such as drive-by downloads, malvertising, and FakeUpdates infections. They use a BLISTER loader to deploy Cobalt Strike beacons for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. Recently, on host identified by `vnevado-win10s` with the AadDeviceId `f5b847aa-8712-4bf6-b4f7-ed6cd89e1505`, a process with ProcessId `6460` was initiated to execute a command to curl a suspicious URL (`http://vectorsandarrows.com`).
question.question: What is the AadDeviceId of the host connected to the end alert which involves the same Manatee Tempest activity group?
solution: There is an activity by the Manatee Tempest group involving an account with AadUserId `731adb71-b11c-4bbf-850b-57989b350e96`.
There is an activity by the Manatee Tempest group targeting a host with AadDeviceId `e5799261-6720-4297-961e-bd9ca4275033`.

[('Manatee Tempest activity group', 'Manatee Tempest activity group', 'The actor that Microsoft tracks as Manatee Tempest is a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

a Russia-based cybercriminal group that has been active since June 2014. It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

For more information, read the Actor Profile: Manatee Tempest Threat Analytics report: https://security.microsoft.com/threatanalytics3/a22c3410-db8f-4c58-866e-ebb760e509d0/analystreport', question.context: As part of a Ransomware infection observed in our organization, file backups were deleted via WMI or VSSAdmin on the host `vnevado-win10r`. The process involved was identified with ProcessId__CreatedTimeUtc__CommandLine `7236__2024-06-20t09:10:51.2193152z__vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all`. Further investigation identified that system recovery setting tampering was observed on the same host, where adversaries might be attempting to delete or remove built-in operating systems data and turn off recovery services to prevent recovering a corrupted system. This may deny access to available backups and recovery options.
question.question: During the system recovery setting tampering, what process and command line was used to disable automatic Windows recovery features?
question.answer: Process Id: 4828, Command Line: `bcdedit /set recoveryenabled no`
solution: An attack was detected where file backups were deleted via `vssblatemp.exe`.

System recovery settings were tampered with using the process `bcdedit.exe` which was launched with the command line `bcdedit /set recoveryenabled no` at `2024-06-20t09:31:59.6743318z` with Process ID `4828`.

The command line used to delete all volume shadow copies on device vnevado-win11t was:
vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all

question.context: A suspicious and anomalous behavior was observed involving a user on device `vnevado-win11t`. This behavior suggested a potential compromise and a series of unusual activities might indicate that this device is involved in a possible human-operated attack by an advanced threat actor. During this investigation, an alert indicating activity from a Russia-based cybercriminal group, Manatee Tempest, was raised. Manatee Tempest is known for their partnership with Mustard Tempest, and they use techniques like drive-by download, malvertising, and FakeUpdates to gain initial access. They proceed with BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike for lateral movement and ransomware deployment, often using domain fronting for command-and-control.
question.question: What is the URL associated with the activity from Manatee Tempest?
solution: The user account `dp5hn` has exhibited suspicious and anomalous behavior on their device.
The URL `vectorsandarrows.com` is associated with the cybercriminal group Manatee Tempest, which uses drive-by downloads and other methods to gain access to target networks.

question.question: Related to this alert, there was also an incident where file backups were deleted. Can you identify the command used in the process that deleted the file snapshots and shadow copies?
solution: A possible attempt to access Primary Refresh Token (PRT) was detected for the AadUserId `731adb71-b11c-4bbf-850b-57989b350e96`.
File backups, including all snapshots and shadow copies, were deleted using process `7236` at `2024-06-20t09:10:51.2193152z` with the command line `vssblatemp.exe delete shadows /all`.

Attackers might be attempting to encrypt content on this device, rendering it unusable to users. This alert links to suspicious hands-on keyboard user behavior observed on the same device. Suspicious and anomalous user behavior might indicate that a user has been compromised. The end alert indicates that unusual activities, such as changes to the frequency and usage pattern of tools or applications, or the user performing a series of unusual activities, were noticed.

Initial detection included the use of PsExec to launch a command on a remote device, suggesting lateral movement using this tool. This was followed by suspicious activities leading to compromised assets exhibiting ransomware-like behavior. The attacker might be using the specified user account, IP, or device to infect multiple devices with ransomware. Automated remediation actions were considered to address the threat.

question.context: As part of a security incident involving the Manatee Tempest activity group, a URL `vectorsandarrows.com` was accessed from the host `vnevado-win11u` using the command `curl http://vectorsandarrows.com`, initiated by process ID 5572 associated with IP address `198.43.121.209`. The actor Manatee Tempest is known for utilizing various methods like drive-by downloads and domain fronting to establish command-and-control channels, and is linked with ransomware deployments facilitated by Mustard Tempest.
question.question: During this investigation, it was also noted that a user account was dropping a ransomware-related file on several devices. Can you identify the name of the ransomware-related file?
solution: The user account with AadUserId `731adb71-b11c-4bbf-850b-57989b350e96` is associated with activity from the Manatee Tempest group, known for its cybercriminal activities and partnerships.

A possible compromised user account is observed dropping a ransomware-related file named `characterical.zip.lockbit` on several devices, indicating potential lateral movement and infection attempts across the network.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.

trajectory.action:
SELECT FileName,
       COUNT(DISTINCT DeviceName) AS DeviceCount,
       GROUP_CONCAT(DISTINCT DeviceName SEPARATOR ', ') AS Devices
FROM DeviceFileEvents
WHERE ActionType = 'FileCreated'
  AND RequestAccountName = 'dp5hn'

A Primary Refresh Token (PRT) is a key artifact of Azure AD authentication on Windows 10, Windows Server 2016 and later versions, iOS, and Android devices. Attackers can attempt to access this resource to move laterally into organization or perform credential theft.

It was notorious for one of its earliest malware lexpaigns – the Dridex banking trojan. Manatee Tempest is also one of the first groups to be sanctioned by the Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) in 2019.

Manatee Tempest’s tactics rely on a partnership with Mustard Tempest, an access broker that facilitates access to target networks. Manatee Tempest has been observed targeting organizations across a diverse array of industries with methods such as drive-by download, including malvertising and FakeUpdates (also known as SocGholish) infections facilitated by Mustard Tempest to obtain initial access, followed by BLISTER loader to deliver Cobalt Strike beacons which are used for lateral movement and ransomware deployment. The actor also uses domain fronting to establish command-and-control channel for Cobalt Strike beacons. Manatee Tempest overlaps with activity tracked by the cyber intelligence industry as EvilCorp, UNC2165, and Indrik Spider.
